title: What is TDD (Test-Driven Development): write the test FIRST (it fails), then write just enough code to make it pass, then refactor: the Red-Green-Refactor cycle: and why does it help (catches bugs early, better design, acts as documentation)?
shortTitle: What is TDD (Test-Driven Development) and the Red-Green-Refactor cycle

s1_definition.oneliner: TDD means write a failing test first, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor, repeating this Red-Green-Refactor loop, which catches bugs early, drives simpler testable design, and leaves tests that document the intended behavior.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Red** – Write one small failing test for behavior that does not exist yet. Confirm it fails for the right reason.
- **Green** – Write the minimum code to make the test pass. Resist adding anything the test does not require.
- **Refactor** – Clean up structure, remove duplication, rename for clarity. Rerun to stay green.
- **Catches bugs early** – Defects detected the instant you write the code, when context is fresh and fixes are cheap.
- **Drives better design** – Writing the test first makes you design from the caller's perspective, producing focused, testable units.
- **Acts as documentation** – Tests are executable specifications that cannot drift out of date because they fail if behavior changes.
s1_definition.analogy: When building the National Bank of India interest calculator, instead of writing the calculator and hoping it works, you first write a tiny check that says "for one hundred thousand rupees at four percent for one year, the interest must be four thousand." It fails because there is no calculator yet, that is Red. Then you write just enough calculator code to make that check pass, that is Green. Then you tidy the code without breaking the check, that is Refactor. You keep adding one small check at a time. The result is that every rule is proven as you build it, the design stays simple because you only write what a check demands, and the checks themselves become a living description of how interest is meant to work.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Test-Driven Development is a practice where I write a failing test before the production code, following the Red-Green-Refactor cycle. Red: I write one small test for a single behavior that does not exist yet and run it to confirm it fails for the right reason, which proves the test really exercises something. Green: I write the minimum code to make it pass, resisting anything the test does not require, because unneeded code is untested code. Refactor: with the passing test as a safety net I clean up the structure, remove duplication, and rename for clarity without changing behavior, rerunning to stay green. Then I pick the next small behavior and loop.

It helps in three concrete ways. It catches bugs early, because a defect is caught the instant I write the code when the context is fresh and the fix is cheap, not later in integration or production. It drives better design, because writing the test first makes me design from the caller's perspective, which produces small focused units with clear interfaces, and hard-to-test code immediately signals a design problem, so TDD naturally pushes toward dependency injection and separation of concerns. And it acts as documentation, because the tests are executable specifications that describe exactly what the code does and which edge cases it handles, and unlike prose they cannot drift out of date because they fail if the behavior changes.

The nuances I add are that TDD is a design discipline as much as a testing one, that tests should target behavior not implementation so refactoring does not break them, that I must see the test fail before making it pass to avoid false confidence, and that it is most valuable for logic-rich code like calculations and rules while applied with judgement for thin glue. At the National Bank of India I used TDD for the interest and fee calculators, writing a failing test for each rule, then the minimal code, then refactoring, and the payoff was both correctness, since a miscalculated fee has real regulatory consequences, and a precise, trustworthy, always-current record of what every rule does. Being able to explain the cycle and tie it to early bug detection, better design, and living documentation is what shows an interviewer I understand TDD as a way to build correct, well-designed, well-documented code rather than a box-ticking ritual.

Remember one sentence: write a failing test first, write the minimum code to pass it, then refactor, and this Red-Green-Refactor loop catches bugs early, drives better design, and creates living documentation.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  TDD Red-Green-Refactor Cycle
  ─────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  RED              │ Write a failing test
  │  Test fails       │ for behavior that
  │  (expected!)      │ does not exist yet
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │
  ┌────────▼─────────┐
  │  GREEN            │ Write the MINIMUM
  │  Test passes      │ code to make the
  │                   │ test pass
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │
  ┌────────▼─────────┐
  │  REFACTOR         │ Clean up structure
  │  Test still passes│ Remove duplication
  │                   │ Keep test green
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │
           └──> Next behavior (loop)
```

keyPoints: TDD means write a failing test first (Red), write just enough code to pass it (Green), then refactor (Refactor)
Red: write one small test for behavior that does not exist yet, confirm it fails for the right reason
Green: write the minimum code to pass, resist adding anything the test does not require
Refactor: clean up structure, remove duplication, rename for clarity, rerun to stay green
Benefits: catches bugs early, drives better testable design, acts as executable documentation that cannot go stale
TDD is most valuable for logic-rich code like calculations and rules, applied with judgement for thin glue code
